To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
encoding wayfinding information interferes with verbal and spatial secondary tasks.
encoding wayfinding information interferes with verbal and spatial working memory, but not with visual working memory.
the working memory systems of verbal and of visuospatial short-term memory were both involved in the wayfinding process.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the human mind is able to store, to recall, and to use spatial and navigational knowledge.
the working memory systems underlying the encoding of wayfinding knowledge in humans.
the cognitive processes involved in wayfinding and with the way in which wayfinding knowledge is encoded in the human mind.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the spatial and the visual secondary tasks are more suitable for wayfinding research than the verbal secondary tasks.
working memory systems are involved in human way finding, but the exact nature of the working memory systems is still unclear.
wayfinding is a complex cognitive task that is based on different working memory systems and that is affected by different kinds of secondary tasks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the spatial secondary task interfered with wayfinding learning, whereas the verbal task did not.
wayfinding knowledge is encoded in a multimodal fashion, with spatial and verbal codes.
the wayfinding task and the verbal and spatial tasks are not independent, and the interference is stronger for spatial than for verbal tasks.
The main takeaway from our work is that
wayfinding knowledge is stored and retrieved in a dual way.
working memory systems are involved in human way finding.
wayfinding is a complex task that is influenced by the working memory system involved in the secondary task.
